introduction-debt-as-a-financial-metapho.core: Technical debt is a financial metaphor: taking a shortcut is borrowing time, and every change to that code pays 'interest' in extra effort until the principal is repaid by refactoring. Debt can be a smart tool or a reckless burden.

first_principles.problem: 'Tech debt' is used to mean 'messy code', so teams can't distinguish strategic shortcuts from negligence or prioritise repayment.
truths: Shortcuts trade future effort for speed now.
Interest accrues when code is touched.
derivation: Recognise debt as a **trade-off**, not just a flaw.
Measure the **interest**: how often it slows you down.

analogy.title: A business loan
analogy.story: A loan to open a shop early can be smart; maxing out credit cards on impulse buys isn't.
analogy.breaks: Code nobody touches accrues little interest, so repaying it may be wasted effort.

steps.label: Insight
steps.detail: Debt taken deliberately and repaid can be a good investment.

check.q: In the tech debt metaphor, what is 'interest'?
check.a: The extra effort spent every time you work with or around the shortcut until it's fixed.

the-quadrant-axes.core: Martin Fowler's quadrant uses two axes: deliberate vs inadvertent (did we know we were taking on debt?) and reckless vs prudent (was it a sound decision?). That gives four types: prudent-deliberate, reckless-deliberate, prudent-inadvertent and reckless-inadvertent.

first_principles.problem: All debt is treated the same, so both strategic trade-offs and skill gaps get the same response.
truths: Intent and judgement are separate dimensions.
derivation: **Reckless + deliberate**: 'no time for design', ignoring consequences.
**Prudent + inadvertent**: 'now we know how it should have been done' (learning).

analogy.title: Four kinds of financial borrowing
analogy.story: A planned mortgage, impulsive payday loans, a loan that looked right until rates changed, and debt from not understanding finance at all.
analogy.breaks: Classification needs honesty, because teams like to label their own debt 'prudent'.

example.title: Classifying four debts
flow: Skipped tests to hit date → reckless-deliberate

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Each one gets the right response.

check.a: Debt discovered through learning, where you later realise a better design that wasn't knowable at the time.

using-the-quadrant-in-practice.core: Use the quadrant to choose a response. Prudent-deliberate debt gets tracked and scheduled repayment; reckless-deliberate needs process and culture fixes (time pressure, standards); prudent-inadvertent needs refactoring as part of normal evolution; reckless-inadvertent needs training, review and mentoring.

first_principles.problem: Teams 'just refactor' everything, but reckless debt keeps reappearing because the cause isn't addressed.
truths: Prevention beats repayment for reckless debt.
Learning debt is natural and healthy.
derivation: **Prudent-deliberate**: debt ticket + repayment date at the time it's taken.
**Reckless-deliberate**: challenge the pressure and enforce minimum standards.

analogy.title: A doctor treating causes, not just symptoms
analogy.story: Different diagnoses need different treatments, even if the symptom (pain) looks the same.
analogy.breaks: Prioritise by interest cost, because classification alone doesn't decide what to fix first.

example.title: A debt review meeting
flow: Tag each debt item with quadrant + interest
Reckless-deliberate cluster → push back on deadline policy

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Less new reckless debt, and smart repayment.

check.q: What's the right response to reckless-inadvertent debt?
check.a: Improve skills and guardrails through training, mentoring, code review and linters, rather than just refactoring.
